note: Behaviour and valuation parameters for the engine's choice model. Every value carries a source and a confidence: high/medium/low/none. Unknown values are null, never invented. Keys are ASCII only (docs/decisions.md D-05).

commuter.source: ABS Census 2016 journey to work (CBD commuting); City of Melbourne Transport Strategy 2030 work-trip focus. Remainder of car-trip mix split by CBD function (work vs retail/services) with VISTA trip-purpose categories.
commuter.note: There is no public table splitting CBD car trips into these four purposes. 0.50 is a working assumption that commuting makes up most car trips: daytime CBD traffic is mainly commuters, and ABS data show jobs are highly concentrated in the CBD. The range is widened to 0.40–0.60. Figures previously quoted here via Huda et al. 2025 (436,752 CBD commuters, 27% by car) were removed because neither could be found in that paper.

local.source: VISTA trip purpose categories (Buy Something / Pick-up or Deliver / Education / social); City of Melbourne Transport Strategy 2030 (local access).
local.note: Local errands, shopping and pick-ups. VISTA has trip-purpose categories but no published four-way split of car trips with a destination in the LGA; 0.25 is a typical order of magnitude for retail and service trips.

tourist.source: City of Melbourne / Tourism Victoria CBD visitor economy reports (qualitative); VISTA social & recreation trip share.
tourist.note: Visitors and leisure. The CBD has many international and interstate visitors, but most walk or take the tram, so their share of car traffic is low. 0.10 is a conservative working assumption.

delivery.source: ABS Survey of Motor Vehicle Use (freight fleet: 84.5% light commercial); O'Fallon & Sullivan light/medium commercial vehicle use in urban centres; Infrastructure Australia Urban Transport Crowding and Congestion (service vehicles).
delivery.note: Delivery and commercial vehicles. The ABS fleet make-up is national, not a share of CBD traffic; delivery plus service vehicles are commonly 10–20% of daytime CBD traffic. 0.15 is the midpoint.

mix_sum_check.note: The four shares must sum to 1 (enforced by test.sh).

generic_warning_divert.source: Working assumption. Literature: Bonsall & Palmer 1999 (book chapter in Emmerink & Nijkamp (eds), Behavioural and network impacts of driver information systems, Ashgate; Routledge reissue https://doi.org/10.4324/9781351119740-9) report early VMS surveys with diversion of 10-80%; Wardman, Bonsall & Shires 1996 (ITS Leeds Working Paper 475, White Rose eprints) cite earlier counts of 5-80%. Messages that recommend a route are assumed to divert more than generic warnings (the Erke 2007 field trial recommended an alternative route).
generic_warning_divert.note: Diversion when the sign only says 'roadwork ahead' and recommends no route. There is no separate field measurement for warning-only messages; 0.03 is the team's working assumption for the engine's two-point calibration (docs/decisions.md D-0929-1435). Wide range; needs measurement.

named_route_divert.source: Erke, Sagberg & Hagman 2007, Effects of route guidance variable message signs (VMS) on driver behaviour, Transportation Research Part F 10(6):447-457. Field trial at two motorway sites outside Oslo, road closure + recommended alternative: about every fifth vehicle changed route (~20%). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trf.2007.03.003
named_route_divert.note: Abstract: “About every fifth vehicle changed route choice according to the recommendation, and almost none drove as far as the closed road section.” The recommended detour was about 70% longer than the main route. Second-hand reports were checked against the original.

stated_to_actual.source: Chatterjee, Hounsell, Firmin & Bonsall 2002, Driver response to variable message sign information in London, Transportation Research Part C 10(2):149-169. Questionnaire stated intention vs observed diversion: only one-fifth of expected drivers actually diverted. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0968-090X(01)00008-0
stated_to_actual.note: Original: “Only one-fifth of the number of drivers diverted compared to that expected from the results of the stated intention questionnaire.” Intended as the discount from stated intention (survey or LLM answers) to actual behaviour. No code reads it: the LLM only reads the sign and the engine's choice model computes the shares (docs/decisions.md D-0929-1435).

hurry.note: How much the driver is in a hurry (engine: multiplies the per-minute utility; mean ≈ 1, range 0.05–5). No public figures per persona; delivery and commuter drivers may be higher, but this is unverified.

familiar.source: Qualitative: commuters use habitual routes (route choice literature); Erke 2007 note that non-diverters knew local network.
familiar.note: Share who know an alternative route. Commuters drive the same route every day, so familiarity is high. Working assumption.

sign_trust.note: No public data on VMS trust rates split into commuter / local / tourist / delivery. Ermagun 2021 (ScienceDirect): higher trust means higher compliance, and trip purpose affects the response, but there are no clean shares.

queue_averse.note: How much the driver avoids queues (engine: multiplies the queue term; range 0–5). No citable figure found for risk preference (lower-priority item P2).

truck_only.note: Restricted to truck routes (boolean). Should be true for delivery vehicles where some roads ban trucks, but whether to set it per persona is undecided; left to the engine and plan side.

hurry.note: How much the driver is in a hurry (engine: multiplies the per-minute utility; mean ≈ 1, range 0.05–5). No public figures per persona; delivery and commuter drivers may be higher, but this is unverified.

familiar.note: Local residents know the CBD network fairly well.

sign_trust.note: As above: no per-persona trust rate.

queue_averse.note: How much the driver avoids queues (engine: multiplies the queue term; range 0–5). No citable figure found for risk preference (lower-priority item P2).

truck_only.note: Restricted to truck routes (boolean). Should be true for delivery vehicles where some roads ban trucks, but whether to set it per persona is undecided; left to the engine and plan side.

familiar.source: Qualitative assumption; tourism wayfinding literature (not cited numerically).
familiar.note: Tourists do not know alternative routes and rely more on signs.

queue_averse.note: How much the driver avoids queues (engine: multiplies the queue term; range 0–5). No citable figure found for risk preference (lower-priority item P2).

truck_only.note: Restricted to truck routes (boolean). Should be true for delivery vehicles where some roads ban trucks, but whether to set it per persona is undecided; left to the engine and plan side.

familiar.source: O'Fallon & Sullivan urban commercial vehicle use (professional drivers know network); qualitative.
familiar.note: Professional drivers know the network, but are pressed by delivery windows.

queue_averse.note: How much the driver avoids queues (engine: multiplies the queue term; range 0–5). No citable figure found for risk preference (lower-priority item P2).

truck_only.note: Restricted to truck routes (boolean). Should be true for delivery vehicles where some roads ban trucks, but whether to set it per persona is undecided; left to the engine and plan side.

legibility_index_m_per_mm.source: NSW TSI-SP-008 Variable Message Signs (standards.transport.nsw.gov.au): legibility distance taken as 700 × letter height (cap height, same units, i.e. 0.7 m per mm). US MUTCD / Access Board: ~35-40 ft per inch letter height (~10.7-12.2 m per 25 mm) is more conservative; AS 4852.1:2019 / AS 4852.2:2019 cover VMS design.
legibility_index_m_per_mm.note: Intended as legibility distance = value × letter height in mm (daytime; lower at night or in bad weather). Known error, not yet corrected: the source's 700 × letter height is 0.7 m per mm, so 25 is about 36 times too high (25 mm letters would read at 625 m instead of 17.5 m). No code reads this parameter.

reading_rate_wps.source: Human factors / VMS message design practice (Austroads Guide to Traffic Management Part 10; NJDOT VMS Operations Manual Dudek 2001). No single Australian mandated wps; 2-3 wps common planning value.
reading_rate_wps.note: How fast a driver reads the sign text. Intended use: legibility distance ÷ speed gives the seconds available, compared with the length of the message. A check on 30 Sep 2026 did not find 2.5 in either cited document, so treat it as an assumption. No code reads this parameter.

max_frames.source: Austroads GTM Part 10 / AS 4852 message design: short messages, few phases preferred.
max_frames.note: Maximum number of frames a VMS message cycles through.

private_car_occupant_aud_ph.source: ATAP Parameter Values / Travel Time (atap.gov.au): private car travel $14.99 per person-hour (40% of Average Weekly Earnings, June 2013 prices). Cited in ATAP research report and BITRE (2025) which uses $35.59/h for some commuter cases — different basis (vehicle vs person, survey year).
private_car_occupant_aud_ph.note: Private car occupant, per person-hour. Vehicle-hour value = per-person value × occupancy.

business_car_occupant_aud_ph.source: ATAP Travel Time: business car travel $48.63 per person-hour (129.8% of AWE, June 2013 prices).

commercial_occupant_aud_ph.source: ATAP Travel Time: commercial vehicle occupants $25.41 (courier/utility) to $28.45 (A-triple/double B-double) per person-hour (June 2013 prices).
commercial_occupant_aud_ph.note: Commercial vehicle occupants, midpoint of the range. The time value of the freight itself is a separate item.

car_occupancy.source: City of Melbourne, Update of the strategic transport evidence base (slide deck; the PDF on AWS is named VISTA_2015-16_Summary): “Car occupancy remains low, with just 1.09 persons per vehicle.” The figure is for work trips to the City of Melbourne from the 2016 Census journey to work, not from VISTA. Cross-check: We Ride Australia submission cites 1.1 average occupancy.
car_occupancy.note: Average occupancy of cars on work trips to the City of Melbourne: 1.09.

private_vehicle_hour_aud.source: Derived: ATAP private $14.99/person-hour × car occupancy 1.09 (City of Melbourne evidence base) ≈ $16.34/vehicle-hour.
private_vehicle_hour_aud.note: Derived value (formula in source). Use this to price delay per vehicle-hour.

queue_aversion.note: Lower-priority item (P2). Queue aversion, i.e. risk preference under uncertain queues; no citable figure found. Song et al. 2025 report that LLMs are more risk-averse than people, but that is not a behaviour parameter itself.

time_of_day_mix.note: Lower-priority item (P2). Persona shares by time of day. VISTA has day and hour, but no persona-by-hour matrix has been built; needs a further split.
